steps.instruction: You're about to build the bootstrap distribution of the mean penny age — resampling the 648 pennies **with replacement** 1,000 times. The original pennies are strongly **right-skewed**. **Before you start, commit to a prediction.**

gate.question: After 1,000 resamples, where will the bootstrap distribution of \(\bar{x}^*\) be centered, and what shape will it take?

choices.text: Centered at the sample mean \(\bar{x}\), and roughly bell-shaped
Centered at the true population mean μ, and bell-shaped
Centered at \(\bar{x}\), but right-skewed like the original pennies

gate.feedback: It centers at **\(\bar{x}^*\)* — the bootstrap only knows your sample, not μ — and comes out **bell-shaped** even though the pennies are skewed. Averaging does that, and we'll come back to why. Now build it and watch.
gate.retryFeedback: The bootstrap resamples from *your sample*, so what's the most it can center on? And what does averaging do to skew?

steps.instruction: Click **+1** once to draw a single bootstrap resample.
steps.observe: Look at the **This Resample** panel. How many pennies were selected once? Twice? Three or more times? How many were not selected at all?
steps.reveal: Because we sample *with replacement*, some pennies get picked multiple times while others are left out entirely. The resample is the same size as the original, but it's not the same pennies.

steps.observe: Did the original sample change? Did the resample change? Is the resample mean different from last time?
steps.reveal: The original sample never changes — it's our real data. But each resample is a new random draw, so the resample mean shifts slightly each time. This is the variability that bootstrapping captures.

steps.instruction: Click the **Play** button and watch the animation for a while.
steps.observe: Watch the histogram build up one bar at a time. What shape is emerging? Where is the distribution centered?
steps.reveal: The bootstrap distribution is approximately **bell-shaped** and centered near the original sample mean — even though the penny ages themselves are right-skewed. Averaging pulls the shape toward symmetry — we'll name why later.

steps.instruction: Click **Pause** to stop the animation. Then click **+1000** to fill out the distribution.
steps.observe: Read the **95% CI** bounds in the results panel. What is the interval? Would you say the average penny age is around 10 years?
steps.reveal: The 95% CI is roughly **(9.7, 11.1)**. We're 95% confident the true mean penny age falls in this range. Since 10 is inside the interval, yes — 10 years is a plausible value for the population mean.

steps.instruction: You've watched the bootstrap distribution of the penny-age mean build up. Put the key ideas in your own words.

prompts.label: Why does the bootstrap distribution center at \(\bar{x}\) (the sample mean) rather than at μ (the true population mean)?
The pennies data are strongly right-skewed, yet the bootstrap distribution of \(\bar{x}^*\) came out bell-shaped. Why?
If you'd started with a different sample of 648 pennies, would the bootstrap distribution be centered at exactly the same place? Would the CI be identical?

respond.answer: A strong answer: the bootstrap resamples from **your one sample**, so it can only know \(\bar{x}\), not μ — it centers on \(\bar{x}\). It comes out bell-shaped even from skewed pennies because it's a distribution of **means**, and averaging invokes the CLT. A different original sample of 648 would center on **its** \(\bar{x}\) and give a slightly different CI — the *method* has 95% coverage, but any single interval is just one draw.
